title: Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP): What It Is and How It Works?
summary: What an ESPP is, how it differs from an ESOP and RSUs, and how India taxes the discount and the sale, with worked rupee examples.
body_markdown:
An employee stock purchase plan (ESPP) lets you buy your employer's shares out of your salary, at a price the plan sets. In India the difference between the shares' value and what you paid is taxed as part of your salary when you buy, and any later rise is a capital gain when you sell. Shares listed only abroad turn long-term after more than 24 months.


If your employer's parent company is listed abroad, the shares you buy are foreign shares. That changes the tax and the paperwork.


## What is an ESPP?


An ESPP is a plan that lets you buy your employer's shares through deductions from your pay, at a price the plan sets, which can be below the market price.


SEBI's rules call the same idea an "employee stock purchase scheme": a scheme under which a company offers shares to its employees. The shares are locked in for at least one year from allotment. These rules cover only companies whose shares are listed on a stock exchange in India.


A foreign parent's plan follows the rules of its own country. Terms such as "qualified plan" or "qualifying disposition" do not decide your tax in India. Here, the Income-tax Act and RBI's overseas investment rules govern you.


## How does an ESPP work, step by step?


You enrol, the plan deducts an amount from each salary for a set period, and on the purchase date the money you have built up buys shares at the plan's price. The exact terms sit in your plan document.


1. **Enrolment.** You choose to join and say how much of your pay goes in.
2. **Deductions.** The amount comes out of each salary and shows on your payslip as a deduction.
3. **Offering and purchase periods.** The offering period is the stretch during which the plan collects your money. The purchase date is the day it turns that money into shares.
4. **Price and discount.** The plan sets the purchase price. A discount is the gap between that price and the market price on the day.
5. **Lookback.** Your plan document says whether your plan has a lookback and how it works.
6. **Shares credited.** The shares land in an account held under the plan.
7. **Hold or sell.** From here the decision is yours.


Your plan document sets what happens to your contributions if you leave the job.


## ESPP vs ESOP vs RSU: what is the difference?


With an ESPP you pay to buy shares, with an ESOP you receive the right to buy at a fixed price later, and with RSUs you receive shares free when they vest.


Vesting is the process by which you become entitled to a grant. An ESOP is an employee stock option: a right to buy shares at a price fixed in advance. An RSU, or restricted stock unit, is a promise of shares that are handed over once they vest, with nothing to pay.


What you get Do you pay? SEBI term? When Indian tax arises


ESPP Shares bought at the plan's price Yes Employee stock purchase scheme Perquisite on the purchase date


ESOP An option to buy at a fixed price after vesting of at least a year, for Indian-listed companies Yes, when you exercise (use) the option Employee stock option scheme Perquisite on exercise


RSU Shares when they vest No Not a SEBI term Perquisite when the shares are allotted to you free of cost


A perquisite is a benefit from your employer that is taxed as part of your salary.


## How is an ESPP taxed in India?


An ESPP is taxed twice: the discount is taxed as part of your salary when you buy, and any rise after that is a capital gain when you sell. A capital gain is the profit on selling something you own.


### When you buy


The perquisite is the market value of the shares on the day, less what you paid. Your employer deducts tax on it, as on the rest of your salary. This is TDS, tax deducted at source before money reaches you. The perquisite is taxed with your salary at your slab rate.


Salary in foreign currency is converted into rupees at the State Bank of India's buying rate for the last day of the month before it is due.


Take an example. Say you buy 10 shares at US$85 each when they are worth US$100 each. The discount is US$15 a share, so US$150 in all. At ₹84 to the dollar, the market value is ₹84,000 and you paid ₹71,400. The perquisite is ₹12,600, added to your salary for the year. The figures are an illustration, not any real plan's terms.


### When you sell


Your cost for working out the gain is the market value that was taxed as salary, which is US$100 a share in the example. The holding period, meaning how long you have owned the shares, starts on the date they were allotted to you.


For shares listed on an Indian stock exchange, a gain is long-term after 12 months. That does not apply to shares listed only abroad. These turn long-term only after more than 24 months. Long-term gains are then taxed at 12.5%, with no adjustment for inflation. Sell sooner and the gain is taxed at your slab rate.


Two rules for Indian shares do not apply here. The ₹1,25,000 allowance and the 20% short-term rate need securities transaction tax (STT) to have been paid, and STT is charged only on trades on Indian exchanges. Section 123 (the old Section 80C) and other deductions cannot be set against the long-term gain.


Convert the gain into rupees at the State Bank of India's buying rate for the last day of the month before you sell. Two assumed examples:


- **Sold after 14 months at US$110.** The gain is US$10 a share, US$100 in all. At an assumed rate of ₹90, that is ₹9,000. It is a short-term gain, taxed at your slab rate.
- **Sold after 30 months at US$130.** The gain is US$300. At an assumed ₹90, that is ₹27,000. It is long-term, so tax is 12.5%, or ₹3,375, plus cess, an extra 4% charge on the tax, of ₹135. The total is ₹3,510, before any surcharge, an extra charge on the tax itself once total income passes ₹50 lakh.


A loss on these shares can be set off only against other capital gains, never against salary. It can be carried forward for 8 tax years if you file your return on time.


### Dividends and tax paid abroad


A dividend is cash a company pays its shareholders out of its profits. Any dividend, from a foreign company too, counts as "income from other sources" and is taxed at your slab rate. It is converted into rupees at the SBI buying rate on the last day of the month before it is declared, distributed or paid.


If foreign tax was taken on income you also pay tax on in India, you can claim a foreign tax credit: the lower of the Indian tax on that income and the foreign tax paid. You furnish a statement in Form 44 within twelve months from the end of the tax year.


## Do you have to report ESPP shares in your tax return?


Yes. If you are resident in India and hold shares or an account abroad at any time in the year, you must file a return and list those foreign assets in it, even if they earned nothing.


Not reporting foreign assets can mean a ₹10 lakh penalty under the Black Money Act. Since 1 October 2024 that penalty does not apply where your foreign assets other than property add up to ₹20 lakh or less.


A sale goes in the capital gains part of your return. For how to file, see[how to file your income tax return](https://koshex.com/blog/income-tax-return-itr) .


## How does your money reach a foreign employer's plan?


Buying a foreign employer's shares under its plan is overseas portfolio investment under RBI's rules. There is no separate cap, but the money counts towards your US$2,50,000 a year under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), and your employer reports the investment.


Under the LRS, a resident individual can remit up to US$2,50,000 a financial year (April to March), and needs a PAN to do it. When a bank sends money abroad under the LRS, it collects TCS, tax collected at source. It is 20% on the part above ₹10 lakh, for purposes other than education or medical treatment. TCS counts as tax already paid, and your employer can adjust it against the TDS on your salary. The full rules are in[TCS on foreign remittances under the LRS](https://koshex.com/blog/tcs-on-foreign-remittance-transactions-under-lrs) .


## What do people weigh up before holding or selling ESPP shares?


Holding keeps your savings and your salary tied to the same company, and that concentration is the main risk to weigh.


- The discount is known on the purchase date. The price afterwards is not.
- The 24-month line changes the tax on a gain, but tax alone is a poor reason to hold or to sell.
- The rupee moves too, so the rupee value of foreign shares changes even when the share price does not.


Your goals, your timeline and how much of your savings already sits in one company all matter.


## How can you spread risk beyond your employer's shares?


By holding investments that do not depend on one company. Examples are diversified equity funds in India, or international funds that hold many foreign companies. Spreading money across many holdings is called diversification.


SEBI has no separate "international" category. Such schemes take two forms. Overseas funds of funds (funds that invest in other funds) keep at least 95% in the underlying fund. Index funds and ETFs track an overseas index, a list of companies picked by fixed rules, with at least 95% in it. Every listed international fund read Very High on the riskometer on 29 September 2026. The riskometer is the six-level risk label SEBI makes every fund show.


An international fund is not taxed like an equity fund. A unit that is not listed on an exchange is long-term after 24 months, taxed at 12.5%. Sold sooner, the gain is taxed at your slab rate. You buy an Indian international fund in rupees, from an Indian fund house, so it is not an LRS remittance.
